answer.sourceLine: Faraday wrote this in his own laboratory journal on 19 March 1849 (entry #10,040), first published in Henry Bence Jones’s The Life and Letters of Faraday, Vol. II (1870), p. 248. The full sentence adds a crucial condition — “if it be consistent with the laws of nature” — that the popular short version drops.

source.excerpt: ALL THIS IS A DREAM. Still examine it by a few experiments. Nothing is too wonderful to be true, if it be consistent with the laws of nature; and in such things as these, experiment is the best test of such consistency.

source.excerptNote: Faraday’s private working note to himself, written while chasing a speculative idea. The famous line is the third sentence — and its force depends on the clause after the comma.

author.name: Michael Faraday
author.heading: About Michael Faraday
author.bio: Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was a largely self-taught English scientist whose discoveries in electromagnetic induction, electrolysis and the field concept underpin modern physics and electrical engineering. A meticulous experimentalist, he kept extensive laboratory journals in which private reflections like this one sit beside his data. The sentence captures his working creed: bold ideas are welcome, but only experiment consistent with natural law can certify them.

misattribution.heading: The wording trap
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Faraday is correct — but the version that travels online is usually mangled.

items.why: The line is very often shortened to just “Nothing is too wonderful to be true,” dropping the conditional “if it be consistent with the laws of nature.” That cut reverses the meaning: Faraday was setting a limit (only what obeys natural law), not celebrating boundless wonder. Wikiquote flags the short form as a partial quotation in its sourced note.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine sentence is conditional — and the condition is the whole point. See the full passage in Life and Letters of Faraday, Vol. II (1870), p. 248.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Faraday wrote these words to himself, not for publication, while pursuing a speculative idea he half-suspected was a fantasy — hence the self-rebuke “ALL THIS IS A DREAM.” The sentence is his answer to his own doubt: don’t dismiss a wonderful idea for being wonderful, but don’t trust it either — test it.

The line has since become a motto for open-minded but disciplined science, engraved above an entrance at UCLA’s Humanities Building. Its staying power comes precisely from the clause the internet keeps deleting: wonder is licensed only by consistency with nature, proven by experiment.
